strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: generating egocentric views of hand-object interactions from a single exocentric image.

The combination of geometric reprojection, hand-pose conditioning, and textual guidance is well motivated. Hand-based depth calibration and alignment provide a practical mechanism for constructing the intermediate sparse view.
Table 1 reports consistent improvements over the evaluated baselines across four H2O settings. For unseen objects, FID improves from 59.615 to 41.334 and LPIPS from 0.4539 to 0.3476 relative to CFLD.
The conditioning ablations support the complementary value of pose and text. Qualitative examples, repeated generations, and explicit failure cases provide useful insight into the method’s behavior.
weaknesses: The quantitative evidence does not clearly validate the central single-image pipeline. Section 4.3 states that H2O uses sparse maps derived from ground-truth depth and relative camera poses, while TACO additionally uses ground-truth hand poses. It does not clearly distinguish training-only use from evaluation-time use. Without explicitly reported results using fully predicted inputs, the benchmarks cannot establish performance without privileged geometry.

The state-of-the-art claim is unsupported by the comparisons. Neither Exo2Ego, the closest single-image competitor, nor 4Diff, which already combines point-cloud projection with diffusion, is evaluated. Comparisons against pix2pixHD, pixelNeRF, and an adapted person-synthesis method are insufficient, particularly without matched conditioning inputs and detailed baseline training protocols.

The generalization protocol is inadequately specified. The 'unseen actions' setting uses the first 80% of frames for training and the last 20% for testing, which does not establish disjoint action categories and may retain substantial sequence overlap. Exact held-out identities, sequence boundaries, sample counts, and split-specific training of the pose estimator are not provided.

The crucial geometry-estimation stage lacks quantitative validation. Appendix A evaluates predicted egocentric hand poses only visually; there are no hand-pose errors, camera-transform errors, depth-calibration measurements, or controlled comparisons between predicted and ground-truth geometry. The source or assumed value of the target camera intrinsics is also unspecified, including for smartphone examples.

Novelty beyond existing geometric reprojection and diffusion pipelines is insufficiently demonstrated. Most components are established models or standard operations, and there is no ablation isolating hand-based scale calibration, estimated camera alignment, or sparse-map conditioning. The reported training procedure also does not substantiate the repeated characterization of the system as end-to-end.

Evidence for broad real-world applicability is limited. TACO results are qualitative and use privileged annotations; the complete pipeline is illustrated with three smartphone examples in a similar setting without egocentric ground truth. Whole-image metrics do not directly establish the claimed accuracy of detailed hand-object interactions, especially when background reconstruction contributes substantially to the gains.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied optimization settings: sampling steps, guidance scale, precise model checkpoints, rasterization details, and baseline adaptations are missing. Overall, the promising reconstruction results do not resolve the major evaluation gaps required for acceptance.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and difficult problem with a coherent pipeline combining geometric reprojection, hand-pose conditioning, textual descriptions, and diffusion-based image completion.
Table 1 reports consistent improvements over the evaluated baselines across four H2O settings. For unseen objects, FID improves from 59.615 to 41.334 and LPIPS from 0.4539 to 0.3476 relative to CFLD.

The conditioning ablations support complementary benefits from pose and text. Qualitative comparisons show promising reconstructions, and the appendix usefully documents failures and sensitivity to incorrect captions.
weaknesses: The benchmark protocol does not establish the central single-image, estimated-geometry claim. Section 4.3 specifies ground-truth depth and relative camera poses for H2O sparse maps, and ground-truth hand poses and sparse maps for TACO, without clearly separating training and evaluation usage. No quantitative comparison of fully predicted versus oracle inputs is provided. Appendix A.1 explicitly states that the proposed pose estimator is unsuitable for TACO.

The closest task-specific methods, particularly Exo2Ego and 4Diff, are discussed but not evaluated. Comparisons against pix2pixHD, pixelNeRF, and CFLD therefore do not substantiate state-of-the-art claims. Baseline adaptation, supervision, and access to equivalent geometric and textual information are insufficiently documented.

The generalization protocol is weaker than claimed. Training on the first 80% of frames and testing on the last 20% does not establish unseen action categories and may retain substantial within-sequence similarity. Exact sequence partitions, sample counts, and confirmation that the pose estimator respects each held-out split are missing.

The geometric contribution lacks quantitative validation. The hand-pose estimator is assessed only visually, with no pose, camera-transform, or reprojection errors. The source of target-camera intrinsics at inference is unspecified, and robustness to occluded hands, scale errors, and ambiguous target viewpoints is not measured.

Novelty is primarily an integration of existing components. The paper does not adequately isolate its advance over prior geometry-aware diffusion and hand-layout-conditioned translation: there is no sparse-map removal ablation or controlled assessment of depth calibration and pose-derived camera estimation.

Evidence for broader applicability is limited. TACO results are qualitative, and the real-world demonstration contains three examples without target-view ground truth. Whole-image metrics do not directly validate the claimed fine-grained hand-object fidelity; interaction-specific measurements or perceptual evaluation are absent.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful optimizer and architecture details: precise data splits, pretrained model variants, sampling settings, baseline training procedures, and uncertainty across runs are not sufficiently specified. Overall, the reported reconstruction gains are promising, but the evaluation gaps leave the main claims below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The task is relevant to egocentric perception and assistive applications. Combining geometric reprojection with pose- and text-conditioned diffusion is a sensible approach to large viewpoint changes and missing visual information.

Table 1 reports consistent improvements over the evaluated baselines across all four H2O settings. For unseen objects, FID improves from 59.615 to 41.334 and LPIPS from 0.4539 to 0.3476 relative to CFLD.

The conditioning ablation supports complementary benefits from pose and text. Qualitative examples demonstrate improved object and background reconstruction, and the appendix usefully documents failures and sensitivity to incorrect descriptions.
weaknesses: The central single-image, calibration-free claim lacks convincing quantitative validation. Section 4.3 specifies ground-truth sparse maps derived from depth and relative camera poses on H2O, and ground-truth poses and sparse maps on TACO. Although introduced as training details, the paper does not clearly distinguish training and test-time conditioning or report an explicit fully predicted benchmark evaluation. Consequently, the quantitative results do not establish the performance of the complete proposed pipeline.

The closest task-specific methods, particularly Exo2Ego and 4Diff, are discussed but excluded from experiments. Comparisons against pix2pixHD, pixelNeRF, and CFLD are insufficient to establish state-of-the-art performance. Matched-input comparisons and a strong diffusion baseline receiving comparable geometric and semantic information are needed.

The generalization evidence is overstated. The H2O 'unseen actions' protocol splits the first 80% and last 20% of frames without establishing disjoint action categories; it therefore does not demonstrate unseen-action generalization. TACO results are qualitative only, and the real-world demonstration comprises three examples in a similar setting without paired targets or systematic assessment.

The key geometric contribution is insufficiently validated. The egocentric pose estimator receives only qualitative evaluation, with no pose, camera-transform, or reprojection errors. There are no controlled tests of depth-scale alignment, sensitivity to pose errors, or the performance gap between predicted and ground-truth geometry. The source of target-camera intrinsics for arbitrary real-world inputs is also unclear.

Novelty beyond integrating existing components is not firmly established. Reprojection followed by diffusion already closely relates to the cited 4Diff approach, while hand-guided translation relates to Exo2Ego. The potentially distinguishing pose-based camera estimation mechanism is not supported by the quantitative analysis needed to demonstrate its contribution.

The metrics do not substantiate the emphasized hand-object interaction fidelity. Whole-image scores can be dominated by backgrounds, as the paper itself notes. Hand-region accuracy, object identity, contact consistency, or a targeted human evaluation would better distinguish plausible synthesis from faithful reconstruction.

Reproducibility is incomplete: exact split identities and sample counts, baseline adaptation and conditioning, diffusion checkpoint and sampling settings, and split-specific training of the pose estimator are insufficiently specified. These omissions make the reported gains and generalization claims difficult to independently assess.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and challenging problem: synthesizing egocentric hand-object interactions from a single exocentric image.

The combination of hand-based geometric alignment, sparse RGB reprojection, and pose/text-conditioned diffusion is well motivated. Qualitative examples show improved scene and object preservation over the evaluated baselines.
Experiments cover four datasets, with substantial supplementary ablations examining conditioning, reconstruction backbones, pose representations, and component removal.
The fully predicted configuration in Table F still outperforms the reported baselines across all six metrics, providing some evidence of practical utility.
weaknesses: The headline evaluation does not clearly substantiate the single-image inference claim. Table F explicitly identifies the exact H2O unseen-action results reported in Table 1 as using ground-truth pose and depth: FID 33.284 and PSNR 31.620. The fully predicted configuration instead achieves 42.323 and 28.897. This materially changes the claimed gains and leaves the input conditions for other headline results unclear. Predicted-input results are needed throughout, with oracle results separately labeled.

The strongest task-specific comparisons are missing. CFLD with ground-truth layouts is not an established upper bound on Exo2Ego, since their architectures and training differ. Removing pose and text from EgoWorld does not reproduce 4Diff's distinct 3D-aware architecture. Consequently, the state-of-the-art claim is unsupported by direct comparisons.

The generalization protocol is insufficiently established. Training on the first 80% of frames and testing on the last 20% does not demonstrate action-disjoint generalization and can retain strong within-sequence correlations. Exact splits, sample counts, and training-versus-testing arrangements for the other three datasets are missing; evaluation on multiple datasets alone does not establish cross-dataset transfer.

Important geometric assumptions remain unresolved. The method requires target-camera intrinsics Kego, but their source or default choice for smartphone examples is unspecified. Predicting target-frame 3D hands from one source image must resolve an ambiguous target viewpoint, yet quantitative camera-transform accuracy and sensitivity to calibration errors are not reported.

Novelty is primarily system integration: point-cloud reprojection and diffusion already appear in closely related work, while the pose regressor, alignment procedure, and conditioning mechanisms use standard components. The incremental contribution needs stronger controlled comparisons against the closest methods.

Reproducibility and robustness evidence are incomplete. Missing details include exact pretrained checkpoints, sampling settings, baseline adaptations, pose-supervision protocols, and detection-failure handling for PA-MPJPE. The manually selected noisy subset has no reported size, and Table F changes the VLM alongside geometry conditions, confounding component attribution. A few smartphone examples without target views provide limited support for broad real-world robustness.

strengths: Addresses a useful, challenging problem: synthesizing egocentric hand-object interactions from a single exocentric image without a reference egocentric frame.

The combination of hand-based geometric alignment, sparse RGB reprojection, and pose/text-conditioned diffusion is technically plausible. Modality and component ablations provide evidence that these cues contribute complementary information.

Experiments cover four datasets and multiple held-out settings. The fully predicted configuration in Table F still outperforms the reported baselines, and the appendix acknowledges meaningful failure cases involving occlusion, finger articulation, and inaccurate captions.
weaknesses: The headline results do not establish performance under the advertised single-RGB-input setting. Table F identifies the exact H2O unseen-action results reported in Table 1—FID 33.284 and PSNR 31.620—as using ground-truth pose and depth. The fully predicted configuration instead achieves FID 42.323 and PSNR 28.897. This materially reduces the claimed gains and requires explicit disclosure and fully predicted evaluations across all settings. Table F also changes the VLM between these configurations, confounding attribution of the difference.

The closest competing methods are not evaluated adequately. CFLD is not demonstrably an upper bound on Exo2Ego merely because it receives ground-truth hand layouts; their architectures and training differ. Likewise, removing pose and text from EgoWorld does not reproduce 4Diff, including its 3D-aware attention. Unavailable source code explains the difficulty but does not substantiate the state-of-the-art claims.

The generalization protocol is insufficiently specified. The H2O 'unseen actions' split uses the first 80% versus last 20% of frames, which does not establish disjoint action categories or independent sequences. Exact splits and sample counts for the other datasets are absent, and it is unclear whether their results involve dataset-specific retraining or cross-dataset transfer. These omissions weaken the central generalization claims.

Important geometric assumptions remain unresolved. The method requires target egocentric intrinsics, but their source for arbitrary smartphone inputs is not explained. Predicting camera-coordinate egocentric hand positions from an exocentric image depends on the target-camera convention, yet robustness to new camera placements is not established. Direct transformation-error measurements and clearer absolute-coordinate pose evaluation would help validate this central component.

Novelty beyond existing geometry-guided diffusion pipelines is limited and insufficiently isolated. The system mainly combines pretrained estimators, standard Umeyama alignment, and conventional latent-diffusion conditioning. The potentially distinctive hand-based camera transformation lacks a convincing comparison against the closest prior methods. Calling the framework 'end-to-end' is also misleading without clarification: the appendix describes separately trained pose and reconstruction models rather than joint optimization.

Evaluation and reproducibility leave substantial gaps. PA-MPJPE removes global pose and scale errors, so it cannot establish correct hand placement or hand-object contact; no direct interaction-fidelity evaluation is provided. The CLIPScore text reference, handling of failed hand detections, sampling settings, and statistical variability are unspecified. Selected unpaired real-world examples support plausibility rather than accurate reconstruction or deployment readiness.

strengths: Addresses a valuable and challenging task: generating egocentric images from a single exocentric image without an initial egocentric frame.

The integration of hand-based geometric alignment, sparse reprojection, and pose/text-conditioned diffusion is well motivated. Qualitative examples show improvements in object appearance and scene reconstruction.
Evaluation spans four datasets and several metrics, with consistent reported improvements over the evaluated baselines. The fully predicted configuration in Table F also outperforms CFLD.
The appendix provides useful component ablations, implementation details, and explicit discussion of failure cases involving occlusion, finger articulation, and inaccurate captions.
weaknesses: The headline evaluation does not clearly support the claimed single-RGB-input setting. Table F identifies the exact H2O unseen-action result reported in Table 1 (FID 33.284, PSNR 31.620) as using ground-truth pose and depth. The fully predicted configuration obtains FID 42.323 and PSNR 28.897, substantially reducing the gains. The input regime for other headline results needs clarification, and fully predicted evaluations are needed throughout. Table F also changes the captioning model between configurations, confounding attribution.

The comparisons do not establish superiority over the closest prior work. Ground-truth-conditioned CFLD is not demonstrably an upper bound on Exo2Ego because the architectures differ. Removing pose and text from EgoWorld does not reproduce 4Diff's distinctive architecture, including its 3D-aware attention. These proxies cannot substantiate the state-of-the-art claim.

The generalization protocol is insufficiently specified. Training on the first 80% of frames and testing on the last 20% does not establish unseen action categories and may retain substantial temporal similarity. The other datasets lack clear split identities, sample counts, and training-versus-transfer descriptions.

The central geometric inference remains under-validated. Predicting target-camera hand coordinates from an exocentric image is inherently ambiguous, yet camera-transform errors and sensitivity to head pose, hand occlusion, and calibration are not quantified. The source of target-camera intrinsics at inference is also unspecified, especially for smartphone examples.

Novelty is primarily the integration of existing estimators, similarity alignment, and diffusion conditioning. Relative to prior geometry-guided diffusion approaches, a stronger controlled comparison is needed to establish the technical advance. The description as end-to-end is also unsupported by the separately trained components.

Reproducibility and metric interpretation remain incomplete: inference settings, precise data partitions, hand-estimator failure handling, and CLIPScore reference texts are not sufficiently documented. PA-MPJPE removes global alignment errors and therefore cannot validate viewpoint accuracy. Selected real-world examples without paired targets provide limited evidence for broad deployment claims.
